In a crowded café, Peter suddenly says that he may have prescribed the wrong insulin dose for a patient and starts describing the patient's details while opening the electronic record on his phone. He asks Zainab to help him calculate the dose. Zainab does not know whether the phone connection is secure, and the patient may already have received the insulin.
sections: Safety & Escalation; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns; Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Communication & Compassion

explanation: Potential administration of the wrong dose creates an urgent safety issue requiring immediate secure escalation.

explanation: Urgency does not remove the duty to limit public disclosure when a secure route can be used immediately.

explanation: This may help clarify the problem quickly, but it should not replace contacting the clinical team through a secure route.

sections: Safety & Escalation; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns; Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Communication & Compassion
action: Whether leaving the café immediately would waste the drinks they bought
explanation: Personal inconvenience is wholly irrelevant to an urgent patient-safety concern.

scenario: Priya is a medical student on placement in a GP surgery. During a consultation, a patient tells the doctor that he stopped taking one of his medications several months ago because it caused severe dizziness. After the consultation, Priya notices that the medication is still listed as being taken regularly on the patient's electronic record. The GP has already called the next patient into the room and appears very busy.
sections: Safety & Escalation; Honesty & Accurate Records; Competence & Supervision
action_a: Priya tells the GP promptly that the medication list may be inaccurate.
action_b: Priya writes herself a reminder and raises it with the GP at the end of the clinic.
action_c: Priya changes the medication list herself without checking with the GP.
rationale_a: A directly protects record accuracy while staying within Priya's role.
rationale_b: B eventually addresses the issue, but an unnecessary delay is less safe than prompt escalation.
rationale_c: C oversteps Priya's authority by altering a clinical medication record independently.

scenario: Matthew is a medical student attending a teaching session. During a break, another student, Daniel, tells Matthew that he has been struggling to cope with the workload and has barely slept for several nights. Daniel says that he is considering skipping his clinical placement for the rest of the week but asks Matthew not to tell anybody because he does not want his tutors to think he is incapable.
sections: Health, Wellbeing & Fitness to Practise; Communication & Compassion; Safety & Escalation
action_a: Matthew asks Daniel whether he feels safe and encourages him to contact appropriate student support.
action_b: Matthew offers to help Daniel reorganise his study schedule and suggests they talk again tomorrow.
action_c: Matthew promises not to tell anyone whatever happens because Daniel asked for privacy.
rationale_a: A addresses both immediate safety and access to appropriate help.
rationale_b: B is supportive but does not adequately assess the severity of Daniel's distress.
rationale_c: C creates an unsafe absolute promise that could prevent necessary escalation.

scenario_title: The Patient Who Wants to Leave
scenario: Leila is a medical student on an emergency department placement. An older patient who has been waiting several hours tells Leila that he is tired of waiting and intends to leave. The patient says that nobody has explained why he needs further tests. Leila knows that the treating doctor has requested blood tests because of concerns about the patient's symptoms.
sections: Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Communication & Compassion; Safety & Escalation
action_a: Leila tells the clinical team that the patient intends to leave and asks someone to explain the reason for the tests.
action_b: Leila asks the patient to wait another thirty minutes while she tries to find the doctor.
action_c: Leila tells the patient he is not allowed to leave until his tests are completed.
rationale_a: A supports autonomy while ensuring the patient can make an informed decision.
rationale_b: B may help practically, but it delays proper explanation and places an arbitrary time request on the patient.
rationale_c: C wrongly restricts a capacitous patient's autonomy.

scenario: Jacob is a medical student having lunch with several other students in the hospital cafeteria. One of them begins telling a humorous story about a patient they saw that morning. The student does not mention the patient's name but gives their age, occupation and an unusual medical condition. Jacob recognises which patient is being discussed.
sections: Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Professional Boundaries & Fairness
action_a: Jacob quietly tells the student that the patient may be identifiable and asks them to stop discussing the case.
action_b: Jacob changes the subject and says nothing else.
action_c: Jacob joins the discussion because everyone at the table is a medical student.
rationale_a: A stops the immediate confidentiality risk and addresses why it is problematic.
rationale_b: B reduces the immediate disclosure but misses the chance to correct the underlying behaviour.
rationale_c: C treats professional status as permission for unnecessary identifiable discussion.

scenario: Aisha is a medical student accompanying Dr Green during a busy ward round. Dr Green asks a junior doctor, Tom, to arrange an urgent blood test for a patient. Two hours later, Aisha passes the patient's bed and learns from the nurse that the blood test has not yet been taken. Tom appears to be dealing with another unwell patient.
sections: Safety & Escalation; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns
action_a: Aisha informs an appropriate member of the team that the urgent blood test is still outstanding.
action_b: Aisha waits until Tom finishes with the unwell patient and then asks whether he knows the test is outstanding.
action_c: Aisha assumes Tom has decided the blood test is no longer needed.
rationale_a: A ensures the urgent task is brought back to clinical attention without blaming Tom.
rationale_b: B is reasonable but may delay action on an explicitly urgent test.
rationale_c: C relies on an unsupported assumption and leaves a safety issue unaddressed.

scenario_title: The Student Asked to Perform a Procedure
scenario: Noah is a medical student on a surgical placement. A doctor asks Noah to remove a patient's wound drain. Noah has watched the procedure several times but has never performed it himself. The doctor tells Noah that it is straightforward and says she will be working at the nurses' station nearby.
sections: Competence & Supervision; Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Safety & Escalation
action_a: Noah explains that he has never performed the procedure and asks for direct supervision with the patient's consent.
action_b: Noah asks another student who has done the procedure once to stand nearby while he performs it.
action_c: Noah performs the procedure alone because he has observed it several times.
rationale_a: A combines appropriate supervision, honesty about competence and patient consent.
rationale_b: B recognises the need for help but substitutes peer reassurance for suitable clinical supervision.
rationale_c: C mistakes observation for competence and creates unnecessary patient risk.

scenario: Sophia is a medical student who has spent several weeks helping to care for Mrs Patel, an elderly patient. On the day Mrs Patel is discharged, she gives Sophia an expensive-looking bracelet and says she wants Sophia to keep it as a thank-you gift. Sophia knows that refusing the gift may upset Mrs Patel.
sections: Professional Boundaries & Fairness; Communication & Compassion
action_a: Sophia thanks Mrs Patel and says she needs to check the rules before accepting an expensive gift.
action_b: Sophia suggests that a card or message of thanks would be more appropriate.
action_c: Sophia accepts the bracelet and keeps the gift private to avoid embarrassing Mrs Patel.
rationale_a: A is transparent, respectful and allows proper guidance to determine what is acceptable.
rationale_b: B maintains boundaries and is good, but it assumes refusal before checking the relevant policy.
rationale_c: C combines a boundary problem with deliberate concealment.

scenario: Ethan is a medical student working with two junior doctors, Hannah and Marcus. During the ward round, Hannah and Marcus disagree about whether a patient's abnormal blood result needs urgent investigation. Their disagreement becomes increasingly heated while the patient is listening.
sections: Teamwork & Colleague Concerns; Communication & Compassion; Safety & Escalation
action_a: Ethan ensures an appropriate senior is aware if the disagreement leaves uncertainty about urgent patient care.
action_b: Ethan later tells his supervisor that the argument in front of the patient was concerning.
action_c: Ethan tells the patient which doctor he thinks is correct.
rationale_a: A prioritises unresolved patient safety while remaining within Ethan's role.
rationale_b: B appropriately addresses professionalism, but it is secondary if the clinical issue itself remains unresolved.
rationale_c: C asks a student to adjudicate and communicate a clinical dispute beyond his role.

scenario: Amelia is a medical student on a hospital ward. The daughter of one of the patients approaches Amelia in the corridor and asks whether her father's scan showed cancer. The daughter explains that her father has asked the doctors not to tell her anything because he does not want her to worry.
sections: Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Communication & Compassion; Professional Boundaries & Fairness
action_a: Amelia explains that she cannot disclose the result and offers to tell the clinical team that the daughter wants to speak with someone.
action_b: Amelia tells the daughter to ask her father directly.
action_c: Amelia hints that the scan is concerning without explicitly stating the result.
rationale_a: A protects confidentiality while responding compassionately and directing the relative appropriately.
rationale_b: B avoids disclosure but is less supportive and may place pressure back on the patient.
rationale_c: C is still a disclosure despite being indirect.

scenario: Imani is a medical student working on a group presentation with three other students. One member of the group, Alex, has arrived late to several meetings and has not completed the section he agreed to prepare. The presentation is due the following morning. Alex messages Imani privately saying that there have been serious problems at home and asks her not to tell the other members of the group.
sections: Teamwork & Colleague Concerns; Communication & Compassion; Health, Wellbeing & Fitness to Practise; Professional Boundaries & Fairness
action_a: Imani asks Alex what support he needs and agrees a realistic plan for completing the presentation while protecting unnecessary personal details.
action_b: Imani quietly completes Alex's entire section herself so the group meets the deadline.
action_c: Imani tells the whole group the details Alex disclosed so they understand why he has not contributed.
rationale_a: A balances compassion, privacy and responsibility to the group.
rationale_b: B solves the immediate task but avoids addressing the problem and unfairly transfers Alex's work to Imani.
rationale_c: C breaches Alex's privacy more widely than necessary.

scenario: Maya is a medical student on a medical ward. During the morning handover, a junior doctor says that a patient had no fever overnight. Maya remembers seeing a temperature of 38.4°C documented at 03:00 while reviewing the notes earlier. The handover has moved on to the next patient, and Maya is not certain whether the doctor has seen the overnight chart.
sections: Honesty & Accurate Records; Safety & Escalation; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns
action_a: Maya checks the chart again quickly and then tells the junior doctor about the recorded fever at the next natural pause in handover.
action_b: Maya immediately interrupts the current patient discussion to say that the junior doctor is wrong.
action_c: Maya waits until the end of the ward round before mentioning the discrepancy.
rationale_a: A verifies the fact and raises it promptly without unnecessary disruption.
rationale_b: B correctly prioritises accuracy but uses a needlessly confrontational and disruptive approach.
rationale_c: C risks allowing inaccurate handover information to influence care for too long.

scenario: Owen is a medical student helping at a GP reception desk. A university friend, Zara, arrives for an appointment and looks surprised to see him. Later, another student who knows Zara asks Owen why she was at the surgery. Owen has not been involved in Zara's care.
sections: Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Professional Boundaries & Fairness; Communication & Compassion
action_a: Owen says he cannot discuss why Zara attended the surgery and changes the subject.
action_b: Owen tells the student only that Zara had an appointment but gives no medical details.
action_c: Owen messages Zara afterwards to tell her that another student was asking why she attended.
rationale_a: A gives no confirmation or detail and cleanly preserves confidentiality.
rationale_b: B still confirms private attendance at a healthcare service without a need to know.
rationale_c: C may be intended as a warning, but it unnecessarily draws Zara into gossip and is less clearly harmful than actually disclosing her attendance.

scenario_title: The Student Who Smells of Alcohol
scenario: Nadia is a medical student due to start an afternoon clinical skills session with her classmate Ben. Ben arrives late and smells strongly of alcohol. He says he had two drinks at lunch but feels completely fine and intends to participate in practising venepuncture on volunteers.
sections: Health, Wellbeing & Fitness to Practise; Safety & Escalation; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns
action_a: Nadia tells the session facilitator privately that she is concerned Ben may be impaired before he practises venepuncture.
action_b: Nadia first asks Ben privately whether he has had anything else to drink and tells him she is worried about him participating.
action_c: Nadia lets Ben take part but watches him closely so she can intervene if he seems unsafe.
rationale_a: A places the immediate safety decision with the responsible facilitator before an invasive task begins.
rationale_b: B is proportionate and supportive, but Ben's admitted drinking and imminent procedure still warrant responsible oversight.
rationale_c: C knowingly permits a potentially impaired student to perform an invasive task and relies on Nadia to manage the risk.

scenario: Daniel is a medical student in an outpatient clinic. A patient speaks limited English. The doctor is delayed, and the patient's adult son offers to translate while Daniel takes a brief history. The clinic normally has access to telephone interpreting, but arranging it may take several minutes.
sections: Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Communication & Compassion; Competence & Supervision
action_a: Daniel asks the patient whether she would prefer the professional telephone interpreter and arranges it before taking a sensitive history.
action_b: Daniel uses the son for simple non-sensitive questions while waiting for the professional interpreter.
action_c: Daniel lets the son translate the full history because the patient appears comfortable and it is quicker.
rationale_a: A best protects accuracy, autonomy and confidentiality.
rationale_b: B may be acceptable for limited practical communication if the patient agrees, but should not replace professional interpretation for a clinical history.
rationale_c: C prioritises convenience over reliable and confidential communication.

scenario: Hannah is a medical student on a surgical placement. A registrar repeatedly invites the same two confident students to scrub into theatre while the rest of the group observes from outside. Hannah has noticed that quieter students have had almost no practical opportunities, although the registrar has not said that participation is restricted.
sections: Professional Boundaries & Fairness; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns; Communication & Compassion
action_a: Hannah asks the registrar privately how theatre opportunities are being allocated and suggests rotating opportunities across the group.
action_b: Hannah encourages the quieter students to volunteer more assertively at the next opportunity.
action_c: Hannah tells the placement lead that the registrar is deliberately discriminating against quiet students.
rationale_a: A clarifies the situation and proposes a fair solution without assuming bad intent.
rationale_b: B may help some students access opportunities but leaves the allocation problem largely unexamined.
rationale_c: C escalates a serious accusation without first establishing whether the pattern has another explanation.

scenario: Marcus is a medical student who has spoken several times with a young adult patient during a two-week placement. On discharge, the patient finds Marcus on social media and sends him a follow request with a message thanking him for being kind.
sections: Professional Boundaries & Fairness; Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Communication & Compassion
action_a: Marcus does not accept the request and, if needed, sends a brief professional message thanking the patient and explaining that he keeps patient relationships off personal social media.
action_b: Marcus leaves the request pending without responding.
action_c: Marcus accepts the request but hides his posts from the patient using privacy settings.
rationale_a: A maintains the boundary while responding courteously.
rationale_b: B avoids an immediate boundary crossing but leaves the situation ambiguous.
rationale_c: C creates the social relationship despite trying to reduce its visibility.

scenario: Amina is a medical student observing a minor procedure. As the team prepares, she notices that the consent form in the notes has not been signed. The patient previously discussed the procedure with the doctor and appears ready to proceed. A nurse says the doctor probably obtained verbal consent and can sign the paperwork afterwards.
sections: Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Safety & Escalation; Honesty & Accurate Records; Competence & Supervision
action_a: Amina alerts the doctor before the procedure and asks that consent be confirmed and documented appropriately before proceeding.
action_b: Amina asks the patient whether they remember discussing the procedure and whether they still want it.
action_c: Amina accepts the nurse's reassurance that verbal consent was probably obtained and says nothing.
rationale_a: A places formal confirmation with the responsible clinician before the procedure begins.
rationale_b: B usefully checks the patient's current wishes but cannot by itself resolve all uncertainty about the consent process.
rationale_c: C relies on an assumption and allows a procedure to proceed with unresolved consent concerns.

scenario: Theo is a medical student travelling home on a bus after placement. Two hospital staff members nearby begin discussing a difficult case, using the patient's first name, age and ward. Theo realises he saw the same patient that day. The staff members do not appear to notice him.
sections: Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Communication & Compassion; Professional Boundaries & Fairness
action_a: Theo discreetly tells the staff members that their conversation can be overheard and that the patient may be identifiable.
action_b: Theo moves to another part of the bus so he cannot hear the discussion.
action_c: Theo listens because he already knows the case and may learn something useful.
rationale_a: A addresses the ongoing confidentiality breach directly and proportionately.
rationale_b: B protects Theo from hearing more but leaves the public disclosure continuing.
rationale_c: C treats educational interest as justification for listening to identifiable confidential information.

scenario: Grace is a medical student in a teaching clinic. A tutor asks whether she would like to examine a patient's abdomen. The patient has already agreed to be seen by students, but the tutor has not specifically asked whether the patient is happy for Grace to perform the examination.
sections: Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Competence & Supervision; Communication & Compassion
action_a: Grace asks the patient directly whether they are happy for her specifically to perform the examination before proceeding.
action_b: Grace relies on the earlier general agreement to student involvement but reminds the patient they can ask her to stop at any time.
action_c: Grace begins the examination because the tutor has asked her to do it.
rationale_a: A obtains specific current consent for Grace's involvement.
rationale_b: B preserves some control but still assumes general consent covers this particular examination and student.
rationale_c: C treats the tutor's request as a substitute for patient consent.

scenario: Isaac is a medical student working with a junior doctor, Lewis. Over several days Isaac notices Lewis make three minor documentation errors, each of which Lewis corrects when it is pointed out. None has caused patient harm. Lewis seems unusually rushed and has been staying late every evening.
sections: Teamwork & Colleague Concerns; Safety & Escalation; Honesty & Accurate Records
action_a: Isaac speaks privately with Lewis about the pattern, asks whether workload is affecting him, and raises it with the supervisor if concerns persist or safety is threatened.
action_b: Isaac reports Lewis immediately for serious misconduct because repeated errors show he is unsafe.
action_c: Isaac keeps correcting the errors himself without discussing the pattern with anyone.
rationale_a: A combines support, fact-finding and proportionate escalation.
rationale_b: B recognises a genuine concern but jumps prematurely to a punitive conclusion not supported by the facts.
rationale_c: C masks the pattern and leaves possible workload or safety problems unresolved.

scenario_title: The Confidential Disclosure With a Safety Concern
scenario: Samira is a medical student in a GP surgery. A 19-year-old patient tells her privately that he has been taking medication prescribed to his housemate for anxiety. He says he sometimes feels faint after taking it and asks Samira not to tell the GP because he is worried the medication will be taken away.
sections: Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Safety & Escalation; Communication & Compassion; Health, Wellbeing & Fitness to Practise
action_a: Samira explains that she cannot promise secrecy where there may be a health risk, encourages the patient to tell the GP and offers to support him in doing so.
action_b: Samira tells the GP immediately without first explaining to the patient that she may need to share the information.
action_c: Samira promises not to tell anyone because the patient is an adult and has asked for confidentiality.
rationale_a: A protects safety while preserving as much autonomy and trust as possible through supported disclosure.
rationale_b: B may ultimately be justified if the risk requires disclosure, but bypassing the patient without explanation is less respectful and proportionate.
rationale_c: C makes an absolute promise that could prevent necessary safety escalation.

scenario: Ravi is a medical student on a ward round. A patient with obesity asks whether a new symptom could be related to her medication. After leaving the bedside, the consultant says, “Most of her problems would disappear if she just lost weight,” and two members of staff laugh. The consultant is also responsible for Ravi's placement assessment.
sections: Teamwork & Colleague Concerns; Professional Boundaries & Fairness; Communication & Compassion
action_a: Ravi seeks confidential advice from an appropriate tutor or placement lead about how to address the consultant's dismissive comments and possible bias.
action_b: Ravi privately tells the consultant that the comment made him uncomfortable and asks whether the patient's medication concern should still be considered.
action_c: Ravi says nothing because challenging the consultant could affect his placement assessment.
rationale_a: A is reasonable and safer for Ravi given the power imbalance, but it may escalate before a direct proportionate conversation is attempted.
rationale_b: B addresses the behaviour and reconnects it to patient care without making an accusation, making it the best first step if Ravi feels able.
rationale_c: C allows fear about assessment to silence a legitimate professionalism and patient-care concern.

scenario_title: The Near Miss That Was Corrected
scenario: Elena is a medical student on a paediatric ward. A junior doctor accidentally prescribes ten times the usual dose of a medication. A pharmacist notices the error before the medicine is administered and the doctor immediately corrects the prescription. The doctor says, “No harm done — there's no point making a fuss about it.”
sections: Honesty & Accurate Records; Safety & Escalation; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns
action_a: Elena encourages the doctor to ensure the near miss is reported through the appropriate safety process and discussed with a senior.
action_b: Elena asks the pharmacist whether the error was serious enough to report before saying anything else.
action_c: Elena accepts that no further action is needed because the medicine never reached the patient.
rationale_a: A recognises that a serious near miss should generate learning even without harm.
rationale_b: B seeks useful context, but the tenfold error is already significant enough that reporting should not depend on the pharmacist's opinion alone.
rationale_c: C mistakes absence of harm for absence of a safety issue.

scenario: Joel is a medical student on an elderly-care ward. A patient with mild dementia refuses a blood test because she dislikes needles. A nurse says, “Her daughter can consent for her — she has dementia anyway.” The daughter wants the blood test to go ahead.
sections: Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Communication & Compassion; Safety & Escalation; Competence & Supervision
action_a: Joel asks an appropriate clinician to assess the patient's capacity for this specific decision and to explore her refusal before any test proceeds.
action_b: Joel asks the daughter to explain why she thinks the blood test is important and then tries to persuade the patient.
action_c: Joel accepts the daughter's consent because the patient has dementia.
rationale_a: A correctly treats capacity as decision-specific and prioritises the patient's own wishes.
rationale_b: B gathers family context but risks turning the daughter into leverage before establishing capacity and the patient's own reasoning.
rationale_c: C wrongly assumes dementia removes capacity and substitutes family consent.

scenario_title: The Confidentiality Request After an Error
scenario: Lucy is a medical student assisting during a procedure. Afterwards, a registrar tells her that he briefly used an item that may not have been sterile, realised immediately, replaced it and believes the infection risk is extremely small. He asks Lucy not to mention it because informing the patient would “only cause unnecessary anxiety.”
sections: Honesty & Accurate Records; Safety & Escalation; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns; Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality
action_a: Lucy tells the registrar the possible sterility breach should be handled through the appropriate clinical and incident process, including senior advice about disclosure.
action_b: Lucy independently tells the patient that a serious sterile-procedure error occurred.
action_c: Lucy agrees not to mention the incident because the registrar believes the infection risk is negligible.
rationale_a: A supports safety, honesty and appropriate disclosure without Lucy overstepping her role.
rationale_b: B prioritises openness but overstates the seriousness and bypasses the responsible clinical process.
rationale_c: C deliberately conceals a possible clinical incident because of hierarchy and a personal risk estimate.

scenario: Kieran is a medical student in an outpatient clinic. A nurse recognises a patient as the parent of a hospital executive and moves them ahead of several people who arrived earlier. The nurse tells Kieran, “It's easier this way — we don't want trouble from upstairs.” There is no obvious clinical urgency.
sections: Professional Boundaries & Fairness; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns; Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality
action_a: Kieran privately asks whether there is a clinical reason for prioritising the patient and, if not, raises the fairness concern with the nurse.
action_b: Kieran says nothing now but later asks a supervisor generally how VIP patients should be handled.
action_c: Kieran accepts the decision because avoiding trouble with senior management is in the clinic's interests.
rationale_a: A checks for information Kieran may be missing before challenging apparent preferential treatment.
rationale_b: B seeks useful guidance but fails to address the immediate unfairness if no clinical reason exists.
rationale_c: C allows status and organisational pressure to override fair access.

scenario: Mei is a medical student on an orthopaedic ward. A physiotherapist asks her to help transfer a heavy patient because other staff are unavailable. Mei has completed basic moving-and-handling training but has never transferred this patient. The patient's notes state that two trained staff and a specific aid should be used.
sections: Safety & Escalation; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns; Competence & Supervision
action_a: Mei explains that the documented transfer plan requires two trained staff and the specified aid, and asks the physiotherapist to arrange this.
action_b: Mei agrees to help if the physiotherapist leads the transfer because the physiotherapist is trained.
action_c: Mei helps with the transfer immediately because delaying it would inconvenience the patient.
rationale_a: A follows the patient-specific safety plan and keeps Mei within her competence.
rationale_b: B recognises the physiotherapist's expertise but still disregards an explicit two-person-and-aid requirement.
rationale_c: C disregards an explicit safety plan for convenience and creates avoidable risk.

scenario: Thomas is a medical student in a sexual-health clinic. A patient asks him a factual question about emergency contraception. Thomas has strong personal objections to emergency contraception and feels uncomfortable discussing it. His supervising clinician is nearby.
sections: Professional Boundaries & Fairness; Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Communication & Compassion
action_a: Thomas tells the patient he is not the right person to advise beyond his competence and promptly asks the nearby supervisor to answer the question without imposing his beliefs.
action_b: Thomas gives only neutral factual information he is confident is accurate, then offers to involve the supervisor for anything further.
action_c: Thomas tells the patient he cannot discuss emergency contraception because it conflicts with his beliefs.
rationale_a: A safely transfers the discussion, but if Thomas can give simple accurate information without compromising care, an immediate handoff may be unnecessarily restrictive.
rationale_b: B preserves patient access while staying factual and within competence, so it is the most balanced response.
rationale_c: C allows Thomas's personal beliefs to obstruct the patient's access to information.

scenario: Fatima is in a private messaging group with students from her placement. Another student posts a photograph of a patient's rash and asks the group what diagnosis they think it is. The patient's face is not visible, but a distinctive tattoo and part of the ward sign can be seen.
sections: Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Safety & Escalation; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns
action_a: Fatima privately asks the student to remove the image immediately and explains that the tattoo and ward sign may make the patient identifiable.
action_b: Fatima saves a copy of the image as evidence before asking the student to delete it.
action_c: Fatima says nothing because the group is private and the patient's face is not visible.
rationale_a: A directly limits further disclosure and addresses the actual identifiability risk.
rationale_b: B may be well-intentioned but creates another unnecessary copy of patient information.
rationale_c: C wrongly assumes a private group and hidden face remove confidentiality concerns.

scenario: Yusuf is a medical student on an evening ward shift. A foundation doctor, Chloe, says she has been working well beyond her scheduled hours because the ward is short-staffed and admits that she is struggling to concentrate. Several prescriptions are still waiting to be completed. Yusuf then sees Chloe enter the wrong patient's hospital number into a prescribing screen before noticing and correcting it.
sections: Health, Wellbeing & Fitness to Practise; Safety & Escalation; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns; Honesty & Accurate Records
action_a: Yusuf speaks to Chloe privately and ensures the senior doctor coordinating the shift is aware that she feels unable to concentrate after an observed prescribing error.
action_b: Yusuf suggests Chloe take a short break while he helps with non-clinical tasks, then reassesses how she feels.
action_c: Yusuf says nothing because Chloe caught the wrong hospital number before submitting the prescription.
rationale_a: A recognises that the combination of self-reported impairment and an observed error requires senior oversight.
rationale_b: B is supportive and may help temporarily, but it should not substitute for a senior decision about fitness to continue safety-critical prescribing.
rationale_c: C ignores ongoing risk merely because one error was caught.

scenario: Aarav is a medical student on a surgical ward. Shortly before an elective procedure, a patient tells him privately that she has been taking her sister's anticoagulant tablets for several weeks because she believed they would prevent a stroke. She stopped taking them two days ago and feels well. She begs Aarav not to tell the surgical team because she is afraid the operation will be cancelled.
sections: Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Safety & Escalation; Honesty & Accurate Records; Communication & Compassion
action_a: Aarav tells the surgical team promptly about the recent anticoagulant use, sharing the clinically relevant details and explaining this to the patient.
action_b: Aarav first asks the patient for the exact drug, dose and last tablet while arranging for the team to be informed immediately.
action_c: Aarav waits to see whether the operation is cancelled before deciding whether the disclosure was necessary.
rationale_a: A makes the time-critical safety information available without unnecessary delay or concealment.
rationale_b: B gathers useful details and can be nearly as good if escalation occurs simultaneously, but the action is slightly less direct.
rationale_c: C delays a potentially critical disclosure for an irrelevant future outcome.

scenario_title: The Competent Patient and Worried Spouse
scenario: Lena is a medical student in a neurology clinic. A patient with capacity has just been told that investigations strongly suggest a serious progressive condition. He asks the team not to tell his spouse yet because he wants time to process the news. In the corridor, his spouse approaches Lena and asks, “Please just tell me whether this is serious. I am the one who looks after him at home.”
sections: Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Communication & Compassion; Safety & Escalation
action_a: Lena tells the spouse she cannot discuss the patient's diagnosis without his permission, but offers to tell the clinical team that the spouse wants support and information.
action_b: Lena asks the patient privately whether he would consider allowing the team to share limited practical information with his spouse about caring for him at home.
action_c: Lena tells the spouse that the condition is serious but avoids naming it.
rationale_a: A protects confidentiality and provides a route for support, but does not explore whether the patient may be willing to authorise limited sharing.
rationale_b: B best respects the patient's wishes while proactively exploring a consensual way to support the spouse.
rationale_c: C still discloses confidential information despite avoiding the exact diagnosis.

scenario_title: The Error Hidden in a Draft Letter
scenario: Nikhil is a medical student helping a registrar prepare discharge paperwork. He notices that a draft letter states the patient's kidney function is normal, although the latest blood results show a significant deterioration. The registrar says the change is “probably temporary” and that the GP will be able to see the blood results electronically anyway. The letter has not yet been sent.
sections: Honesty & Accurate Records; Safety & Escalation; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns; Competence & Supervision
action_a: Nikhil tells the registrar that the discharge letter should accurately reflect the latest kidney results before it is sent and seeks senior review if the registrar refuses.
action_b: Nikhil adds the abnormal result to the draft himself and leaves the registrar to notice the change before signing it.
action_c: Nikhil allows the letter to be sent because the GP can access the blood results electronically.
rationale_a: A directly addresses the inaccurate record through the responsible clinician and provides proportionate escalation.
rationale_b: B corrects the content but makes an unauthorised change rather than resolving the issue transparently with the responsible clinician.
rationale_c: C accepts a misleading letter because another information source exists.

scenario: Mariam is a medical student. A close friend sends her a photograph of a changing skin lesion and asks, “Does this look like melanoma to you?” The friend says the next routine GP appointment available is in two weeks and is very anxious.
sections: Professional Boundaries & Fairness; Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Competence & Supervision; Communication & Compassion
action_a: Mariam tells her friend she cannot diagnose the lesion from a photograph, explains that a changing lesion should be professionally assessed, and helps her identify an appropriate route for timely review.
action_b: Mariam says it does not look like melanoma to her but advises the friend to see a GP anyway.
action_c: Mariam forwards the photograph to a dermatology registrar she knows and asks informally what they think without first getting her friend's permission.
rationale_a: A stays within competence while taking the friend's concern seriously and facilitating appropriate care.
rationale_b: B gives potentially false reassurance from an inadequate basis and exceeds Mariam's competence.
rationale_c: C breaches privacy by sharing the image without permission and seeks informal specialist advice outside a proper care pathway.

scenario_title: The Senior Asks for a Backdated Entry
scenario: Jonah is a medical student on a ward. A senior doctor realises she forgot to document an important discussion she had with a patient the previous afternoon. Jonah was present for the discussion. She asks Jonah to enter a note under yesterday's date because, she says, “You heard it too, so it is accurate.” The electronic system would make the entry appear as though Jonah wrote it yesterday.
sections: Honesty & Accurate Records; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns; Safety & Escalation
action_a: Jonah tells the senior doctor he can confirm he witnessed the discussion but will only document it as a current, clearly dated late entry if authorised and appropriate.
action_b: Jonah refuses to write anything and tells the doctor she must document the discussion herself.
action_c: Jonah enters the note under yesterday's date because the content itself is accurate.
rationale_a: A preserves both factual content and the integrity of the time and authorship of the record.
rationale_b: B protects record integrity but may be unnecessarily rigid if Jonah can make an honest, authorised late entry about what he witnessed.
rationale_c: C falsifies when the entry was made even though the underlying conversation occurred.

scenario_title: The Patient Refusing One Student After Consent
scenario: Sofia is a medical student on a surgical placement. A patient previously signed a form agreeing to student involvement. Immediately before anaesthesia, the patient recognises Sofia from a local gym and says he is uncomfortable with Sofia personally being present, although he is happy for other students to remain. The surgeon looks irritated and says the patient already consented to students.
sections: Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Communication & Compassion; Professional Boundaries & Fairness
action_a: Sofia tells the surgeon that the patient has specifically withdrawn consent for her involvement and leaves the procedure area.
action_b: Sofia asks the patient once, privately and without pressure, whether he is certain he does not want her present, then accepts the answer.
action_c: Sofia remains because the earlier signed form covered student involvement and the procedure is about to begin.
rationale_a: A immediately respects the patient's current specific refusal.
rationale_b: B is respectful if genuinely non-coercive, but the patient's refusal was already clear, so asking again risks creating subtle pressure.
rationale_c: C treats prior general consent as irrevocable and ignores a current specific refusal.

scenario_title: The Colleague Pattern Without an Incident
scenario: Ibrahim is a medical student working regularly with another student, Chloe. Over two weeks Chloe has become forgetful, missed two teaching sessions and once arrived at the wrong ward, but Ibrahim has not seen her make a clinical error. Chloe tells him she is sleeping about three hours a night because of serious family problems and asks him not to tell the medical school because she fears being removed from placement.
sections: Health, Wellbeing & Fitness to Practise; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns; Safety & Escalation; Professional Boundaries & Fairness
action_a: Ibrahim speaks privately with Chloe, encourages her to seek support immediately and tells her that if he remains concerned about her ability to function safely he will need to involve an appropriate tutor.
action_b: Ibrahim agrees to keep the situation private for 48 hours if Chloe promises to sleep and attend all sessions.
action_c: Ibrahim reports Chloe immediately for being unfit to practise without first speaking to her or seeking proportionate advice.
rationale_a: A balances support, transparency and proportionate escalation in a developing but not yet proven clinical-risk situation.
rationale_b: B recognises Chloe's need for support but creates an arbitrary delay despite signs that may already affect safe functioning.
rationale_c: C is not the least appropriate because escalation may eventually be necessary, but immediate punitive reporting without proportionate assessment is still poor.

scenario: Keira is a medical student helping with an approved clinical audit. A registrar sends her a spreadsheet containing patient names and hospital numbers and asks her to work on it at home using her personal laptop. The audit only requires anonymised data. The hospital has a secure remote system, but the registrar says it is slow and tells Keira that using personal email will be quicker.
sections: Honesty & Accurate Records; Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Professional Boundaries & Fairness; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns
action_a: Keira tells the registrar she will only use the secure hospital system and asks for the dataset to be anonymised before she accesses it remotely.
action_b: Keira downloads the file to her personal laptop but deletes names and hospital numbers immediately before doing any analysis.
action_c: Keira emails the identifiable spreadsheet to her personal account because the registrar has authorised it and the secure system is slow.
rationale_a: A uses the authorised route and minimises identifiable data from the outset.
rationale_b: B reduces identifiability after download but still transfers sensitive data onto an unauthorised device first.
rationale_c: C uses an insecure route for identifiable data merely for convenience.

scenario_title: The Patient Refusal and Family Pressure
scenario: Adam is a medical student on an oncology ward. A patient with advanced cancer has capacity and has repeatedly declined an invasive investigation because she says she would not want further treatment regardless of the result. Her adult children privately tell Adam that they believe she is making a mistake and ask him to persuade her, saying she listens to medical staff more than to them.
sections: Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Communication & Compassion; Safety & Escalation
action_a: Adam confirms that the patient understands the consequences of refusing and supports the clinical team in ensuring her decision remains informed and voluntary.
action_b: Adam tells the patient that her children are very worried and asks whether she would reconsider the investigation for their sake.
action_c: Adam agrees with the children to keep encouraging the patient until she changes her mind.
rationale_a: A respects a capacitous refusal while ensuring it is informed rather than simply accepting or challenging it.
rationale_b: B acknowledges family concern but introduces pressure unrelated to the patient's own values.
rationale_c: C repeatedly pressuring a capacitous patient to reverse a settled decision undermines autonomy.

scenario_title: The Ambiguous Safety Concern in Public
scenario: Zainab is a medical student leaving the hospital with a junior doctor, Peter. In a crowded café, Peter suddenly says that he may have prescribed the wrong insulin dose for a patient and starts describing the patient's details while opening the electronic record on his phone. He asks Zainab to help him calculate the dose. Zainab does not know whether the phone connection is secure, and the patient may already have received the insulin.
sections: Safety & Escalation; Teamwork & Colleague Concerns; Consent, Autonomy & Confidentiality; Communication & Compassion
action_a: Zainab stops the public discussion and asks Peter to contact the ward immediately through a secure route to confirm whether the insulin was administered and obtain senior clinical advice.
action_b: Zainab asks whether the insulin has already been given before deciding whether they need to contact the ward urgently.
action_c: Zainab helps Peter calculate the dose at the café table because immediate safety outweighs confidentiality.
rationale_a: A addresses confidentiality and urgent patient safety simultaneously.
rationale_b: B asks a relevant question, but making escalation conditional on the answer may waste time when a serious error is already possible.
rationale_c: C handles urgent safety in a public, insecure way and asks a medical student to substitute for appropriate clinical review.
